slides.title: Defining Who Medical Affairs Engages
bullets: Defines deliberately who the organization needs to engage, and how
Structures relationships according to each actor's role and influence
Translates the KOL mapping and segmentation work into strategic planning

slides.title: A Broader Stakeholder Ecosystem
bullets: Digital opinion leaders, whose influence runs through online channels
Scientific and professional societies that shape guidelines and consensus
Patient associations, who surface unmet needs and quality-of-life gaps
Emerging investigators and, in many markets, payers and HTA assessors

slides.title: From Mapping to Differentiated Relationships
bullets: Start from situational analysis of who is influential and how positioned
Combine it with influence-level segmentation from earlier KOL mapping work
Top-tier KOLs get a longitudinal, high-contact, bidirectional relationship
Broader specialist segments get reach through education and digital channels

slides.title: One Ecosystem, Many Functions
bullets: MSLs, market access, scientific communication, and RWE teams share the ecosystem
Without coordination, one KOL can be over-contacted from multiple fronts
Or, just as damaging, no team owns the relationship with a relevant actor

slides.title: A Guide for Limited Relational Time
bullets: Not every possible contact merits the same level of investment
The stakeholder strategy shows where to invest limited relational time
Understanding the logic behind it means executing with judgment, not just a list

takeaway.title: Stakeholder strategy turns KOL mapping into a deliberate plan for who gets what relationship
bullets: The relevant ecosystem is wider than clinical KOLs alone
Relationship intensity should match each segment's role and influence
Cross-functional coordination prevents both overload and ownership gaps
